extracted.intended_audience: writers, artists, critics, and general readers interested in literature, art, gender and cultural criticism (early-20th-century magazine readership)
extracted.subtask_description: Prescriptive and critical statements about what makes good art, literature, architecture, illustration, and choice of work — emphasizing content over mere style, social (vs. personal) expression, gender balance in artistic production, and fidelity of illustration to text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance of masculinity and femininity in the arts
rubrics_metrics.description: Too great a predominance of masculinity degrades many arts; examples include the degrading spectacle of the 'dancing girl' and a pervasive one-sided masculine influence across arts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Excess masculine dominance produces egoism and an over-emphasis on personal sensation and display rather than social or humane expression. The author argues that many contemporary defects in dance, sculpture, music, poetry, and literature stem from this imbalance and that a 'nobly equal womanhood' would change the artistic product.

rubrics_metrics.name: Domestic architecture should express women's and children's needs
rubrics_metrics.description: The home is essentially a place for the woman and the child; yet the needs of woman and child are not expressed in our domestic architecture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Current houses are built on industrial precedent (kitchen as working centre) and as physical expressions of proprietorial family limitations. For domestic architecture to be beautiful it must 'truly express simple and natural relations' and grow in larger beauty as lives develop; the failure to design homes around women's and children's needs explains the low aesthetic level of ordinary dwellings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sculpture requires free, equal womanhood and recognition of the human body
rubrics_metrics.description: Sculpture has been injured by the degradation of the human body, vicious standards of sex-consciousness enforced under the name of modesty, and covered ugliness which inhibit free high work in sculpture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Only with 'a nobly equal womanhood, stalwart and athletic' and higher standards of beauty and decorum can sculpture produce different, higher work. The text links social attitudes toward women's bodies and modesty directly to the quality of sculptural art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Art should prioritize social/human expression over self-expression
rubrics_metrics.description: The main evils of a too masculine art lie in the emphasis laid on self-expression; the tendency to self-expression instead of social expression disfigures art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critique of the 'ultra-masculine' artist who paints to make others feel how he personally was affected rather than to express for humanity. The higher the artist, the broader his vision and the less personal (less 'ultra-masculine') his expression; art should make broader human experience visible, not merely the artist's private sensations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Literature's basic merit is the idea/content, not mere skill of expression
rubrics_metrics.description: The basic merit in literature, as in speech, lies in the thing said. Literature preserves and transmits ideas and feelings; style and skill should be subordinate to content.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An eloquent speaker or writer who delights merely by form ('She's a beautiful talker!') still must be judged by what she says. Even fiction that is 'picture-work' must carry a certain content of ideas or it 'does not make sense.' This rule is used to judge the modern magazine's output and to condemn empty verbal virtuosity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of 'pure literature' and critique of the 'novel without a purpose' idea
rubrics_metrics.description: A quoted high-critical view: 'Pure literature must perforce be a form of expression, but must not condescend to express anything.' Thus 'the Novel With a Purpose' is scorned by certain arbiters of taste, who prefer novels 'without a purpose.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author questions this ideal: is the 'Novel Without a Purpose' genuinely preferable? She uses the Peterkin Papers anecdote to satirize the notion that art must be purposeless to be 'pure,' implying that such a standard is elitist and obstructs the expression of contemporary ideas and social issues in literature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understand the modern magazine as a different medium with differing standards
rubrics_metrics.description: The modern magazine is a new product — a halfway-house between the newspaper and the book — and serves as a fluent, popular mouthpiece rather than exclusively as a storehouse of 'beautiful letters.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because magazines aim to serve readers with limited time/money, they publish practical informative pieces ('articles about flying machines') and a large mass of fiction that the austere critic may refuse to call 'literature.' Writers and critics should recognize that magazine publication operates under different demands and audiences than book publication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allowance for purposeful or controversial literature
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'guardians of this noble art' condemn and exclude what they define as 'controversial literature' (stories advocating contested social ideas), even when they print fiction that upholds popular positions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author argues this is inconsistent and biased: if controversy is a discussion with two sides, magazines should not systematically refuse stories presenting the less-popular or reformist side. Literature should have room to express the new ideas and feelings of the time rather than be censored by canons of taste rooted in the past.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choosing work: personal fitness and social demand guide vocation
rubrics_metrics.description: In choosing work there are two governing factors: (1) personal fitness (instinctive specialization) and (2) the social demand — the call of the work that needs doing — with a third factor often being pressing necessity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If free to choose and not rigidly specialized, one should 'look about and see what other people need' and take hold of some social need (e.g., better school board, forest preservation). Work is both social service and personal development; study the local environment and select tasks that serve society.

rubrics_metrics.name: Illustration should reflect the author's vision — 'middle-sized' artist ideal
rubrics_metrics.description: A good illustrator ought to know pretty much everything and be able to make pictures like the picture the author saw; big artists prefer to make their own images, little artists cannot realize another's; the ideal is a 'middle-sized artist' who can do both.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrators who care more for their own vision than the author's can produce mismatches (wrong hair color, wrong mood). The best illustrations 'leave nothing to be desired' and reinforce the text (examples: Tenniel, Dore). Publishers and artists should seek illustrators able to translate the author's mental image faithfully while possessing adequate independent skill.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of the female figure in allegory should emphasize strength and universality, not ornament
rubrics_metrics.description: When artists express noble social ideas (Truth, Justice, Liberty), they frequently use the woman's body as the highest human type; the artist, being true to humanity, gives a strong, grand figure, 'beautiful indeed, but never decorated.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allegorical figures based on women should avoid trivial ornamentation ('Fancy Liberty in ruffles and frills, with rings in her ears--or nose') and instead present a dignified, human form suitable to convey universal ideals.
